verdict.rationale: The phrase mia ton sabbaton, the first of the week, recurs across seven New Testament passages (Matt 28:1, Mark 16:2, Luke 24:1, John 20:1, John 20:19, Acts 20:7, 1 Cor 16:2), and in the four gospel occurrences it explicitly marks the resurrection morning, which is a dense and stable lexical pattern. Acts 20:7 attaches that same first-day phrase to a corporate gathering synegmenon to break bread, and Rev 1:10 supplies the only canonical adjective kuriakos applied to a day. However the lexemes themselves do not legislate primacy: kuriakos (G2960) is near-hapax with two NT occurrences and does not on its own specify which day; mia ton sabbaton uses sabbaton (G4521) as the counting term for week without ever declaring a binding shift from the seventh day; and Col 2:16, Rom 14:5, and Gal 4:10 affirmatively warn against judging by sabbaths or by reckoning days, which is the lexical hinge for a no-special-day reading. So the first-day rhythm and the resurrection-morning association are lexically dense, but the further claim that this is the appointed gathering day is a synthesis the words permit rather than impose.

scripture.force: The date phrase te mia ton sabbaton, the first of the week, frames a gathering (synegmenon, perfect passive participle of synago) whose stated purpose is to break bread (klasai arton). This is the clearest lexical link between the first day and a corporate assembly, but the day is named only by its position in the week, with sabbaton serving as the counting term, and the verse does not legislate a reason such as honoring the resurrection or assign primacy over any other day.

Kata mian sabbatou, on the first of every week, governs an instruction that each person (hekastos) set aside and store up (thesaurizon) for a collection (logeia) par heauto, by himself. The temporal marker matches the first-day phrase of Acts 20:7, yet the action described is individual home laying-aside rather than a corporate worship act, so the verse supports a first-day rhythm of the believer's life but does not by itself establish an appointed gathering on that day.

Egenomen en pneumati en te kuriake hemera, I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, supplies the only canonical use of kuriakos (G2960) applied to a day. The adjective means belonging to or pertaining to the Lord, parallel to its only other NT use kuriakon deipnon, the Lord's supper, in 1 Cor 11:20. The lexeme itself does not specify which calendar day, so equating te kuriake hemera with the first day is an inference from canonical context, not a fact the word alone carries.

Ouses oun opsias te hemera ekeine te mia sabbaton, on the evening of that first day of the week, the disciples are together behind shut doors when the risen Christ stands among them. The same mia sabbaton phrase recurs, and the scene places a resurrection appearance on the first day, supplying the narrative basis for associating that day with the resurrection. The text reports an event, however, and does not legislate a recurring appointed day.

Opse de sabbaton te epiphoskouse eis mian sabbaton, after the sabbath, at the dawning toward the first of the week, places the discovery of the empty tomb on the first day. The mia sabbaton phrase is fixed here in a resurrection setting, which is one of four gospel attestations of the same construction marking the same calendar moment.

Te de mia ton sabbaton Maria he Magdalene erchetai proi, on the first of the week Mary Magdalene comes early, again uses the mia ton sabbaton phrase to mark the resurrection morning. Combined with Matt 28:1, Mark 16:2, and Luke 24:1, the four gospels lexically converge on this exact phrase as the moment of the resurrection report.

Me oun tis humas krineto en brosei kai en posei e en merei heortes e neomenias e sabbaton, so let no one judge you in food and drink or in respect of feast or new moon or sabbaths. The lemma sabbaton (G4521) appears in a list of calendar markers the Colossians are instructed not to be judged by, which is the lexical hinge for a reading in which no calendar day is binding on the believer.

Hos men gar krinei hemeran par hemeran, hos de krinei pasan hemeran. hekastos en to idio noi plerophoreistho, one esteems one day over another, another esteems every day alike; let each be fully convinced in his own mind. The lemma hemera (G2250) is paired with krino, to judge or esteem, and the verse explicitly assigns the matter to individual conviction (plerophoreistho), which the no-special-day reading uses as a direct lexical complication to any appointed-day claim.

Hemeras paratereisthe kai menas kai kairous kai eniautous, you observe days and months and seasons and years. The verb paratereo (G3906) carries the sense of observing scrupulously, and the catalogue of time units is given a negative cast in the surrounding rebuke. This text constrains how strong an appointed-day claim can be lexically pressed without colliding with the apostolic warning.

complicating_texts.resolution: The phrase kata mian sabbatou marks the first day, but par heauto titheto, let each set aside by himself, describes individual home storage for a logeia rather than a corporate assembly. This complicates the appointed gathering claim and is addressed by observing that the verse establishes a first-day rhythm and pairs with the corporate gathering of Acts 20:7, while the gathering element itself rests on Acts, not on this verse.

Kuriakos (G2960) names a day belonging to the Lord but does not lexically identify which day, so the verse cannot by itself prove first-day primacy. This is addressed by treating Rev 1:10 as neutral evidence: it attests a named Lord's day in the canon, and combining it with the mia ton sabbaton texts identifies the day, but the identification is canonical inference rather than lexical equation.

The counting term inside the date phrase is sabbaton (G4521), the same lexeme used for the seventh-day sabbath, which a seventh-day reading exploits to argue the sabbath term is never displaced. This is addressed by observing that mia ton sabbaton is an idiom where sabbaton means week, not the sabbath day, and the action assigned to the first day here is the gathering to break bread, distinct from any seventh-day rest observance.

Sabbaton (G4521) is listed alongside feast and new moon as items by which the believer is not to be judged. The first-day reading addresses this by noting that the prohibition concerns judgmental imposition of Mosaic calendar observance, not the spontaneous emergence of a new first-day pattern; the no-special-day reading takes the same verse as ruling out any calendar day having binding status. Both readings are lexically defensible from the words themselves.

The text explicitly assigns day-esteem to individual conviction (plerophoreistho, fully convinced in his own mind), which prima facie complicates an appointed-day claim. It is addressed by limiting the verse to disputed-matters territory and by noting that mia ton sabbaton in Acts 20:7 is treated as practice rather than as judgmental imposition, but the no-special-day lens reads Rom 14:5 as the controlling principle that any binding appointed-day language overreaches the lexical data.

Paratereo (G3906) is used negatively for observing days, months, seasons, years. This is addressed by reading the warning as targeting return to Mosaic-calendar observance under compulsion, leaving a free first-day pattern lexically unaddressed by the verse; the no-special-day lens takes it as a general caution that any prescribed day risks the same critique. The words themselves do not adjudicate which scope is intended.

Sabbatismos (G4520) is a New Testament hapax that redirects sabbath imagery to an eschatological rest entered by faith. This neither prescribes nor abolishes a weekly day, and is addressed by noting that the lemma reframes sabbath as participation in God's rest rather than calendar observance, which is compatible with either a first-day reading or a no-special-day reading and therefore does not settle the question.

variants.note: The orchestrator bundle reports no variant units bearing on the date phrase or on kuriakos, and not_in_ecm_scope is true for these NT passages outside 3 John. The apparatus marks in the supplied text (raised dots on hemon in Acts 20:7, ean in 1 Cor 16:2, mia in John 20:19) do not touch the lemmas that carry the verdict, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Combines the four-gospel resurrection-morning attestation of mia ton sabbaton (Matt 28:1, Mark 16:2, Luke 24:1, John 20:1) with the first-day evening gathering of John 20:19, the first-day breaking of bread in Acts 20:7, the weekly first-day giving rhythm of 1 Cor 16:2, and the named kuriake hemera of Rev 1:10. On this reading the lexical pattern is dense enough that the first day is the appointed Christian assembly day in honor of the resurrection, even though no single verse legislates it as such.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: no special day prescribed (Rom 14, Col 2 reading)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Holds that Rom 14:5 assigns day-esteem to individual conscience (plerophoreistho), Col 2:16 explicitly forbids letting anyone judge in respect of sabbaths, and Gal 4:10 warns against observing days, months, seasons and years. On this reading the first-day texts attest practice and freedom, not a binding appointment, and the kuriake hemera of Rev 1:10 names a day belonging to the Lord without prescribing it for the church.

Argues that sabbaton (G4521) remains the counting term in every NT date phrase and is never lexically displaced by a new legislated day; that the Decalogue command (Exod 20:8) stands; and that 1 Cor 16:2 concerns home storage rather than corporate worship. On this reading the first-day texts describe occasional practice rather than a binding shift of the appointed day.

hermeneutics.notes: All three lenses can be derived from the same lexical data without doing violence to the words. The first-day reading is supported by the convergence of mia ton sabbaton with resurrection narrative and with gathering verbs, the no-special-day reading is supported by the Pauline freedom texts, and the seventh-day reading is supported by the non-displacement of sabbaton as a counting term. The verdict turns on synthesis rather than on any single lexeme.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Examine how the New Testament uses the phrase mia ton sabbaton (first of the week) and the adjective kuriakos (Lord's), and what day, if any, the texts associate with Christian gathering and with the resurrection.
stem_audit.notes: The original stem asserts three loaded conclusions at once: that the first day is appointed, that it is the gathering day, and that the reason is honoring the resurrection. The lexical data attests first-day gathering as practice (Acts 20:7, John 20:19), a fourfold gospel association of the first day with the resurrection morning, and a named Lord's day (Rev 1:10), but does not lexically supply the appointed status or the stated honor-the-resurrection rationale as a binding prescription. The verdict was derived on the original stem; the neutral rephrasing is recorded only to expose the embedded assumptions.

lay_summary: The question hangs on a small set of New Testament texts that point in a consistent direction without nailing every claim shut by themselves. The Greek phrase mia ton sabbaton, the first of the week, appears in all four gospels at the resurrection morning (Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:2, Luke 24:1, John 20:1), in the evening gathering of John 20:19 where the risen Jesus appears, in Acts 20:7 where believers come together to break bread, and in 1 Corinthians 16:2 where Paul tells each person to set money aside on that day. Revelation 1:10 then gives the only place where a day is named the Lord's day, using the adjective kuriakos, which simply means belonging to the Lord and does not by itself say which calendar day is meant. Two lexical facts explain why this still ends up disputed. First, the word that counts the days, sabbaton, is the same word used for the sabbath, so a seventh-day reading argues the older day was never replaced. The reply is that mia ton sabbaton is an idiom where the word means week, not sabbath. Second, three other passages cut directly against any binding day. Colossians 2:16 says let no one judge you in respect of sabbaths, Romans 14:5 says one esteems one day above another, another esteems every day alike, let each be fully convinced in his own mind, and Galatians 4:10 rebukes those who observe days and months and seasons and years using a verb (paratereo) for scrupulous observance. So three readings can stand on the words themselves: a first-day reading that treats the convergence of resurrection morning, evening gathering, weekly giving, and the named Lord's day as decisive; a no-special-day reading that treats day-esteem as a matter of conscience; and a seventh-day reading that holds the sabbath term was never displaced. The plain words support a real first-day pattern of meeting and a clear resurrection-morning association, yet the fuller claim that the first day is appointed and that its purpose is to honor the resurrection has to be assembled from several passages rather than read off any single verse. That is the lexical root cause of the dispute: a dense pattern combined with explicit freedom texts that the words themselves do not rank.
